newsitem.title: LEBANON: FEATURE - Women's group tackles Lebanese wife-beating.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Women's group tackles Lebanese wife-beating.

text.p: "Every house has its secret," says an Arab proverb, and it took Samia only a few days to discover that her new neighbours' secret was wife-beating.
Since the middle-aged couple moved into an apartment on the floor above hers in a crowded Beirut district the routine has been the same almost every night, Samia said.

The husband returns home at around midnight. For a while he paces angrily in the apartment while Samia, on the floor below, anticipates the first slap. Shortly afterwards, the wife is weeping out on the balcony.

Samia, a young professional woman, lives alone. Her brother dissuaded her from going to the police to denounce the case, fearing she might endanger herself. Instead, she got involved in a new womens' rights movement: The Lebanese Council to Fight Violence Against Women.
TALES OF HORROR, IN PRIVATE

In Lebanon, mere discussion of domestic violence is considered taboo, but in private women exchange endless stories of wife-beating or express horror at rape incidents occasionally buried in local newspapers.
Women activists told Reuters they believe male violence is widespread at all levels of post-war Lebanese society.
A judge at a Beirut Moslem religious court said around 10 percent of 5,000 divorce lawsuits filed by women over two years were the outcome of physical violence by their husbands.
Outside the court, a 38-year-old woman who asked not to be identified told Reuters her husband had beaten her for 10 years, ever since they got married.

"I have reported it to the police several times. They always cooled me down and handed me over to my husband who would promise not to beat me again. They never agreed to start formal proceedings for me. Now I am here to see a judge," she said.
WOMEN DOUBLE VICTIMS IN WAR AND PEACE
Zoya Rouhana, president of the Council to Fight Violence Against Women, says Lebanese women are being forced back into their traditional role since the 1975-90 civil war ended.
"It is unfortunate to see Lebanese women, who carried the burden of war like the men, forced to revert to their traditional role, which imposes other forms of violence on them," she said.
The council, formed in April, this month launches its first public awareness campaign telling Lebanese women they can get help and legal consultation if they are abused.
The council also organises hearings at Lebanon's first "listening centre" in Beirut. Counsellors and a hotline are available with numbers advertised on television.

The idea of listening centres where a group of women get together to share painful experiences, sob their hearts out and discuss ways out of their dilemmas was first introduced to the Arab world in north Africa.

"In recent weeks, we received 10 cases on the hotline, almost all related to domestic violence and beating. Women asked for appointments with our lawyers who gave them consultancy on their legal options," activist Dia Saleh told Reuters.
COUNCIL TELLS WOMEN THEY HAVE OPTIONS
The council includes social workers, psychiatrists, journalists and lawyers, who volunteer their time to help women.
"We want to tell women they have options. The issue at stake here is the right of human beings to life, to free choice, to self-determination," Saleh said.
In May, the council held the first public hearing in Lebanon at which a battered woman told of her experience.
"She managed to overcome her fear and...stand in front of an audience to urge women to stand up for their rights and reject constant humiliation," activist Hanan Ghazi said.
"She wanted to tell women that taking a husband to court was not the worst thing a woman could do, as society claims. It is simply a legitimate way of asking for her rights," she added.
Council members believe the only way to counter violence is by acknowledging it and fighting it, Rouhana told Reuters.
LEGAL REFORMS URGED

Rouhana and 35 activists from 18 different NGOs make up the founding committee of the council, which has high on its agenda improving women's legal literacy, updating laws to protect women, and providing statistics on violence against women.
"When we first came together, we realised that each of us knew in her social circle at least one woman who was violated, mainly beaten by her husband," Rouhana said.
She believed many Lebanese women accepted violence and humiliation in silence because obtaining a divorce was often difficult for both Moslems and Christians.
Rouhana said the council would ask the government to train policewomen to handle complaints by women because abused women were often subjected to psychological pressure at police stations.

The council will also seek the abolition of Lebanese laws on "crimes of honour" which exempt close male relatives from punishment if they kill a daughter, wife or sister they suspect of having love affairs.
"The so-called 'honour crimes' are strong evidence of womens' subordinate legal position, which justify, though indirectly, violent acts against them," Rouhana said.
